```text
# Handoff: where codemap came from, what's decided, what's next

Context for anyone (person or agent) picking codemap up. The code and `README.md` say *what* exists; this says *why*,
what was learned along the way, and what's still open. As of 2026-11-02.

## 1. The problem

When you build mostly by directing AI agents, you lose your model of the system. Fixes become band-aids: each change is
judged locally ("did the error go away?") rather than against how the system is meant to work, and nobody notices the
same spot being patched five times. Call it **comprehension debt**: code that exists but that no person understands.

The founding example is real. On an EHR workflow builder (care journeys, journey templates, automations such as "send
this email after the patient converts"), the concepts kept getting rewired, and the frontend looked finished. It was
impossible to tell how the backend was wired, or whether it was wired at all. *"I just trusted what I saw on the
frontend."*

## 2. Who it's for

- **Main user: semi-technical builders who ship with agents.** They know enough to act on what a map shows ("nothing
  listens for this event" is obviously a bug), but can't hold the whole system in their head. This group is growing
  fastest.
- **Not fully non-technical people.** They want "make it work and don't make me think about the backend", which works
  against the product. They're also mostly inside Lovable, Replit or Bolt, which own the screen.
- **Not senior engineers, mostly.** They already hold the model. The exception is an unfamiliar codebase.
- **Buyer later: teams and eng leads** worried about agent-written code nobody understands.
- **Framing:** it's not "leveling the playing field". It's "stay in control of what your agent builds, and get better
  at it as you go."

## 3. What people said (Oct 2026 interviews)

- **Jay** struggles with UX iteration; that's a different product, so leave it out. Separately, he worries whether V1 will
  hold up for V2 and V3, and has no visibility into the backend his technical cofounder owns. That suggests **the map as
  a shared language between a non-technical founder (who views and asks) and a technical cofounder (who acts).**
  Promise "you'll see where V2 will hurt", not "you'll know it scales".
- **The integration interviewee is the clearest signal.** He had to change a client's data integration, asked GPT how
  the workflow worked, and got a wall of text instead of a diagram. *Consultants working in client codebases* may be a
  sharp segment: they hit this on every new client.
- **The third person** plans heavily and says AI implements well "but…". The note cut off. **Follow up**: this is either
  the toughest customer or evidence that the pain is smaller for disciplined planners.
- **The bar to clear is "ask Claude for a Mermaid diagram".** That's free and solves maybe 60% of "wall of text". Codemap
  has to win on things people notice: claims checked against the code, click-through to the code, the same drawing every
  time, and **showing what's missing**.

## 4. What the user wants from the interface (direct feedback)

- **Point at anything and ask.** Select a box, an arrow or a region; answers appear next to what was selected.
- **Plain English first.** Translating code into concepts *is* the value. Three depths: Concept, How it works, Code.
  Define jargon. Use a small concrete example from their own code.
- **A real graph:** areas as containers, steps inside, labeled arrows between them. An early design with lane rows of
  blocks was rejected as "unintuitive, not an actual graph".
- **A walkthrough written with each map,** because a graph alone is hard to start reading. Stops go in the order that
  makes sense to a newcomer, and you can ask at every stop.
- **No "guess what happens next" prompts.** That idea was rejected.
- **The agent can fix things from the map**, not just explain them (see decision 5).
- **Model-agnostic is wanted.** The simplest version: codemap runs its own Claude explainer, and any coding agent
  launches it.
- **Learning from walkthroughs:** a diagram of the user's own vibecoded architecture lost them. Every diagram needs its
  question and a line of context on top, 5 to 7 boxes at first with details on click, and plain labels.

## 5. Design decisions and why

1. **v1: Claude explores, a plain program checks.** No deterministic graph engine yet, because it isn't needed for
   "ask, get a map". Claude explores with Read/Grep/Glob and returns the map in a fixed format. `check()` re-reads every
   cited line and verifies calls, requests and imports against code facts. Later, the engine can replace the explorer
   behind the same format.
2. **The map format (`packages/core/src/format.ts`) is the one-way door.** Everything else is replaceable. Statuses are
   never stored; they're computed on every check.
3. **"Nothing does X" is a claim with proof.** Absences carry the search that proves them, and the checker reruns it.
   The missing connection is the bug people care about, and only a graph that can show absences can show it.
4. **Codemap runs its own Claude explainer,** separate from the user's coding chat. It works with any agent and keeps
   explanation quality consistent. It can read the whole repo: the map is a starting point, not a fence. Anything it
   adds is drawn only if the checker confirms it.
5. **Fixes:** Claude proposes. The fix is drawn as a green dashed arrow next to the exact diff. Nothing changes until
   approval. Then codemap writes exactly that diff, refusing if the files changed since the proposal, re-checks the map,
   and offers Undo. Only one agent edits at a time. If codemap is ever connected to the user's coding chat, that agent
   makes the edit instead.
6. **Delivery:** the basic version works everywhere through a skill, the `codemap` CLI and a browser tab. Optional
   upgrades (not built):
   - **Channels:** Claude Code only, research preview. An MCP server pushes the user's question into the running chat.
   - **MCP Apps:** Cursor, VS Code Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude Desktop. The viewer embeds in the chat, and `ui/message` sends
     questions.
   - **Codex:** no documented way to push into a running session. Its desktop app has a Browser with an Annotate picker
     and WebMCP, which might allow something similar; untested.
7. **Local only:** binds to 127.0.0.1, a token is required, Host and Origin are checked, and secrets are never read.

## 6. Graphify, for comparison (github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify, read at v0.9.97)

- **Agent-facing.** Code goes to a graph through tree-sitter (no LLM). Query is keyword match, then BFS spreading in every
  direction. Clusters (Leiden) are named after their busiest node. Updates happen after commits, asynchronously, in
  seconds. There are no ordered flows, no fetch → route links, and no events or queues for JS. Its "benchmark" measures
  tokens, not task success. Graphify Cloud (YC S26) adds architecture rules.
- **Ideas worth borrowing:**
  - An edge counts as EXTRACTED only with import evidence; ambiguous matches are dropped rather than guessed.
  - Edges belong to the file they come from, so a change evicts only that file's edges.
  - Keep cluster IDs stable between rebuilds.
  - Stamp the graph with `built_at_commit`.
  - Hook messages phrased as facts, not commands. They found imperative wording gets ignored as prompt injection.
- **Don't build on it.** Codemap's edge is everything it lacks.

## 7. What's built (verified)

- **Tests:** four packages, 102 tests, no model calls.
- **Viewer:** tested in Chrome with scripted Claude (`npm run preview`): making a map, the walkthrough, select and ask,
  a follow-up that adds checked steps, a fix (approve, reload, undo).
- **Real Claude, on the care-app fixture:**
  - The map came back 20 of 20 confirmed on the first pass, for about $0.21.
  - It also found a bug nobody planted: nothing ever starts the nightly job.
  - A real question cost about $0.14 and added two confirmed gaps.
  - A real fix cost about $0.24, was approved and applied, and re-checked 22 of 22.
- **Demo frontend:** `examples/care-app-ui/index.html`, the patient app as staff see it. Convert a patient and no welcome
  email arrives, even though the automation is active.

## 8. Not built yet, and next steps

- **Undo for an applied fix lasts only while the server runs.** Questions, answers and fix states are saved with the
  map (since 2026-11-03), and simple questions are answered from the map before Claude searches the code.
- **Hand-off to the user's coding agent** (channels / MCP Apps) and an MCP `publish_map` tool for agents that explore on
  their own.
- **Big repos are untested.** The head-start scan reads the whole repo.
- **Next, in order:**
  1. **Run Phase 0 with the integration interviewee:** his real question, codemap vs "Claude + Mermaid" side by side.
  2. Try codemap on a real repo, or a fresh Scout copy (`../scout-run`; never `../scout-agent`).
  3. Done 2026-11-03: off-topic questions offer a new map (or an answer in words), plus a map switcher. Next there: a
     routing test of 10–15 real questions with expected routes, run by hand since it uses Claude.
  4. Channels hand-off in Claude Code.
  5. MCP Apps.
- **Later (Phase 3 of the plan):**
  - A fast graph engine with updates on every edit (incremental, LSP-style).
  - Live agent activity on the map.
  - "Working somewhere you haven't explored" and a per-user explored-regions map.
  - "This step was patched 5 times this week" counters. That's the *band-aid detector*, and it needs a time dimension.

## 9. Gotchas that cost time

- **Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` 0.3.296), verified from its types:**
  - The call is `query({ prompt, options: { cwd, model, tools, allowedTools, permissionMode: 'dontAsk', settingSources: [], strictMcpConfig, outputFormat: { type: 'json_schema', schema }, resume, hooks } })`.
  - The answer arrives as `structured_output` on the `result` message.
  - PreToolUse hooks can return `permissionDecision` and `updatedInput`.
  - Auth is an API key or the Claude Code login.
- **React Flow 12:**
  - With controlled nodes, measurements live on `getInternalNode(id).measured`, not on your node objects.
  - Nodes that aren't selectable or draggable get `pointer-events: none` unless `onNodeClick` is set. Steps carry
    `nopan` so a pan doesn't swallow clicks.
- **ELK:** spacing options apply per container, so each area repeats them.
- **Chrome automation:**
  - A hidden tab renders no React Flow edges and drops input; check `document.visibilityState` and drive the page with
    in-page events.
  - The first click after a navigation is often dropped.
- **zsh `echo` mangles backslashes in JSON.** Write curl output to a file instead.
- **Channels with a custom server:**
  - Launch with `claude --dangerously-load-development-channels server:<name>`.
  - Claude Code won't register a channel server on MCP protocol 2026-07-28; `MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1` works around it.
  - The page needs its own sender check (a token): an ungated channel is a prompt-injection risk.

## 10. Links

- Design spec, current: [Codemap v1 Design](https://claude.ai/artifact/55L8tokprGe61qtfpDXJ5h)
- Longer-term plan with the engine: [Point-and-Ask Architecture](https://claude.ai/artifact/7hWiwFyugpB6hT6x3DKoJs)
- Graphify vs. ours: [Two Code Graphs Compared](https://claude.ai/artifact/8u9v9BAXW4pTLkz72exhv5)
- Early concept frames (Figma): https://www.figma.com/design/i8aTiDS47Eb68QeoKvQopW
- Hackathon origin, reference only: `../Speedhacks-project` (the Interpretability harness)
- Claude Code channels: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/channels · MCP Apps client matrix:
```

```text
// The map format: what Claude (or later the engine) writes, the checker verifies and the viewer draws.
// This is the one-way door. Statuses are never part of it: the checker computes them from the repo every time.
import { z } from 'zod';

const Id = z.string().regex(/^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,64}$/, 'ids use letters, digits, _ . : - (at most 64)');

/** A line of code that backs a claim. `text` must appear on that line (whitespace-insensitive) or within a few lines of it. */
export const Evidence = z.object({
  file: z.string().min(1),
  line: z.number().int().positive(),
  text: z.string().min(1).max(400),
});

/** How a box is drawn: a way in (button, route, CLI), a step, a store (table, queue), something outside the repo, a job. */
export const NodeKind = z.enum(['entry', 'step', 'store', 'external', 'job']);

/**
 * What an arrow claims. `calls`, `request` (fetch → route) and `imports` are also proven from code facts;
 * `then` (and anything the extractors can't see yet, like events) is proven by its evidence text alone.
 */
export const EdgeKind = z.enum(['calls', 'request', 'imports', 'then']);

export const Area = z.object({ id: Id, label: z.string().min(1).max(40) });

export const Node = z.object({
  id: Id,
  area: Id,
  kind: NodeKind.default('step'),
  name: z.string().min(1).max(80),
  /** `<file>#<symbol>` as the facts name it, e.g. `src/patients/service.ts#markConverted`. */
  symbol: z.string().regex(/^[^#]+#.+$/, 'symbol is <file>#<name>').optional(),
  explain: z.object({ concept: z.string(), how: z.string(), code: z.string() }).partial().optional(),
  evidence: z.array(Evidence).min(1),
});

export const Edge = z.object({
  id: Id,
  from: Id,
  to: Id,
  kind: EdgeKind.default('then'),
  label: z.string().min(1).max(60),
  evidence: z.array(Evidence).min(1),
});

/** A claim that something is missing, proven by a search the checker runs again: `matches` is the count claimed. */
export const Absence = z.object({
  id: Id,
  claim: z.string().min(1).max(200),
  /** Draw it as a missing arrow between these boxes. */
  between: z.object({ from: Id, to: Id }).optional(),
  search: z.object({
    pattern: z.string().min(1).max(200),
    regex: z.boolean().default(false),
    /** Globs to search; the whole repo when omitted. */
    paths: z.array(z.string().min(1)).optional(),
  }),
  matches: z.number().int().min(0),
});

export const TourStop = z.object({
  id: Id,
  title: z.string().min(1).max(80),
  text: z.string().min(1).max(1200),
  focus: z.object({
    areas: z.array(Id).optional(),
    nodes: z.array(Id).optional(),
    edges: z.array(Id).optional(),
    absences: z.array(Id).optional(),
  }),
  terms: z.array(z.string()).optional(),
  ask: z.array(z.string()).optional(),
});

export const CodeMap = z.object({
  version: z.literal(1),
  question: z.string().min(1).max(300),
  /** The commit the map was made from, when known. */
  commit: z.string().nullable().optional(),
  areas: z.array(Area).min(1),
  nodes: z.array(Node).min(1),
  edges: z.array(Edge).default([]),
  absences: z.array(Absence).default([]),
  tour: z.array(TourStop).default([]),
});

export type Evidence = z.output<typeof Evidence>;
export type MapNode = z.output<typeof Node>;
export type MapEdge = z.output<typeof Edge>;
export type MapAbsence = z.output<typeof Absence>;
export type TourStop = z.output<typeof TourStop>;
export type CodeMap = z.output<typeof CodeMap>;

export type ParseResult = { ok: true; map: CodeMap } | { ok: false; problems: string[] };

/** A repo-relative path that can't climb out of the repo: no absolute paths, no `..`, no backslashes. */
export function isSafeRelativePath(path: string): boolean {
  if (!path || path.startsWith('/') || path.includes('\\') || /^[A-Za-z]:/.test(path)) return false;
  return path.split('/').every((seg) => seg !== '..' && seg !== '');
}

/** Validates shape, then references: unique ids, edges between real boxes, tour stops that point at real things. */
export function parseMap(input: unknown): ParseResult {
  const parsed = CodeMap.safeParse(input);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { ok: false, problems: parsed.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join('.') || '(map)'}: ${i.message}`) };
  }
  const map = parsed.data;
  const problems: string[] = [];
  const ids = (kind: string, items: readonly { id: string }[]) => {
    const seen = new Set<string>();
    for (const { id } of items) {
      if (seen.has(id)) problems.push(`${kind} id "${id}" is used twice`);
      seen.add(id);
    }
    return seen;
  };
  const areas = ids('area', map.areas);
  const nodes = ids('node', map.nodes);
  const edges = ids('edge', map.edges);
  const absences = ids('absence', map.absences);
  ids('tour stop', map.tour);

  const evidence = (where: string, list: readonly Evidence[]) => {
    for (const e of list) if (!isSafeRelativePath(e.file)) problems.push(`${where}: evidence file "${e.file}" must be a path inside the repo`);
  };
  for (const n of map.nodes) {
    if (!areas.has(n.area)) problems.push(`node "${n.id}": unknown area "${n.area}"`);
    if (n.symbol && !isSafeRelativePath(n.symbol.slice(0, n.symbol.indexOf('#')))) problems.push(`node "${n.id}": symbol file must be a path inside the repo`);
    evidence(`node "${n.id}"`, n.evidence);
  }
  for (const e of map.edges) {
    if (!nodes.has(e.from)) problems.push(`edge "${e.id}": unknown node "${e.from}"`);
    if (!nodes.has(e.to)) problems.push(`edge "${e.id}": unknown node "${e.to}"`);
    evidence(`edge "${e.id}"`, e.evidence);
  }
  for (const a of map.absences) {
    if (a.between && !nodes.has(a.between.from)) problems.push(`absence "${a.id}": unknown node "${a.between.from}"`);
    if (a.between && !nodes.has(a.between.to)) problems.push(`absence "${a.id}": unknown node "${a.between.to}"`);
  }
  for (const t of map.tour) {
    const refs: [string, readonly string[] | undefined, Set<string>][] = [
      ['area', t.focus.areas, areas], ['node', t.focus.nodes, nodes], ['edge', t.focus.edges, edges], ['absence', t.focus.absences, absences],
    ];
    for (const [kind, list, known] of refs) for (const id of list ?? []) if (!known.has(id)) problems.push(`tour stop "${t.id}": unknown ${kind} "${id}"`);
  }
  return problems.length ? { ok: false, problems } : { ok: true, map };
}
// The checker: decides which claims in a map the code actually backs. It reads the repo and never writes. One function,
// used everywhere a map reaches a person: when it's published, on every answer, when a saved map is reopened, after a fix.
// No model calls. Python and Go facts need `initTreeSitter()` to have been awaited once; TS/JS needs nothing.
import {
  DEFAULT_IGNORE,
  createFactsIndex,
  fileExistsIn,
  findFetchSites,
  listRepoFiles,
  matchRoute,
  matchesAny,
  settleCalls,
  squash,
  symbolNames,
  type CallFact,
  type FileFacts,
} from '@codemap/facts';
import type { CodeMap, Evidence, MapAbsence, MapEdge, MapNode } from './format';
import { createRepoReader, isSecretPath, type RepoReader } from './repo';

export type Status = 'confirmed' | 'unconfirmed';
/** `fact`: the extracted code facts back the claim. `text`: the cited lines say what the claim says. */
export type Proof = 'fact' | 'text';
export type EvidenceCheck = { file: string; line: number; ok: boolean; foundAt: number | null; reason: string | null };
export type ClaimCheck = { status: Status; proof: Proof | null; evidence: EvidenceCheck[]; reasons: string[] };
export type AbsenceCheck = { status: Status; found: number; locations: { file: string; line: number }[]; reasons: string[] };
export type TourCheck = { status: 'ok' | 'mentions-unconfirmed'; unconfirmed: string[] };
export type CheckReport = {
  nodes: Record<string, ClaimCheck>;
  edges: Record<string, ClaimCheck>;
  absences: Record<string, AbsenceCheck>;
  tour: Record<string, TourCheck>;
  summary: { claims: number; confirmed: number; unconfirmed: number };
};
export type CheckOptions = {
  /** Extra globs to leave out of searches (build output and `.codemap/` are always left out). */
  ignore?: readonly string[];
  /** How far a cited line may have moved and still count (default 3). */
  lineWindow?: number;
};

const MAX_LOCATIONS = 20;

export function check(map: CodeMap, root: string, options: CheckOptions = {}): CheckReport {

  for (const a of map.absences) absences[a.id] = checkAbsence(a, repo, files());

      ...(t.focus.edges ?? []).filter((id) => edges[id]?.status !== 'confirmed'),
      ...(t.focus.absences ?? []).filter((id) => absences[id]?.status !== 'confirmed'),

// Route paths and file-based routes (Next.js). Pure and browser-safe.
import type { RouteFact } from '../contracts/facts';

export const HTTP_METHODS = ['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS'];

/**
 * Normalize a route path so ids are stable: params (`:id`, `{id}`, `[id]`, `[...x]`, regex groups `([\w-]+)`) become `{}`,
 * regex anchors and escapes are dropped, and a leading `/` is ensured.
 */
export function normalizeRoutePath(raw: string): string {
  let p = raw.trim().replace(/^\^/, '').replace(/\$$/, '').replace(/\\\//g, '/');
  p = p.replace(/\((?:[^()\\]|\\.)*\)\??/g, '{}'); // regex capture groups
  p = p.replace(/\[\[?\.{0,3}[^\]/]*\]?\]/g, '{}'); // [id], [...slug], [[...slug]]
  p = p.replace(/:[A-Za-z_$][\w$]*\??/g, '{}').replace(/\{[^}/]+\}/g, '{}').replace(/\{\}[+*?]+/g, '{}');
  p = p.replace(/(^|\/)\*+(?=\/|$)/g, '$1{}');
  p = p.replace(/\\(.)/g, '$1').replace(/\/+/g, '/');
  if (!p.startsWith('/')) p = `/${p}`;
  return p.length > 1 ? p.replace(/\/$/, '') : p;
}

export const routeId = (method: string, path: string) => `route:${method} ${path}`;

export function routeFact(method: string, rawPath: string, file: string, handler: string | null): RouteFact {
  const m = method.toUpperCase() === 'ALL' ? 'ANY' : method.toUpperCase();
  const path = normalizeRoutePath(rawPath);
  return { id: routeId(m, path), method: m, path, file, handler };
}

const NEXT_APP_ROUTE = /(?:^|\/)app\/((?:.*\/)?)route\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$/;
const NEXT_APP_PAGE = /(?:^|\/)app\/((?:.*\/)?)page\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$/;
const NEXT_PAGES = /(?:^|\/)pages\/(.*)\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$/;

/** URL path for a Next.js segment list: route groups `(x)` and slots `@x` drop out. */
const segmentsToPath = (dir: string) =>
  normalizeRoutePath(`/${dir.split('/').filter((s) => s && !/^\(.*\)$/.test(s) && !s.startsWith('@')).join('/')}`);

/** Next.js file-based routes and pages for `path`, given its export names. Handlers are symbol names in the file. */
export function nextRoutes(path: string, exportNames: readonly string[]): { routes: { method: string; path: string; symbol: string }[]; page: string | null } {
  let m = NEXT_APP_ROUTE.exec(path);
  if (m) {
    const url = segmentsToPath(m[1]!);
    return { routes: exportNames.filter((n) => HTTP_METHODS.includes(n)).map((n) => ({ method: n, path: url, symbol: n })), page: null };
  }
  m = NEXT_APP_PAGE.exec(path);
  if (m) return { routes: [], page: segmentsToPath(m[1]!) };
  m = NEXT_PAGES.exec(path);
  if (m) {
    const rest = m[1]!.replace(/(?:^|\/)index$/, '');
    if (/^api(?:\/|$)/.test(rest)) return { routes: exportNames.includes('default') ? [{ method: 'ANY', path: segmentsToPath(rest), symbol: 'default' }] : [], page: null };
    if (/(?:^|\/)_(?:app|document|error)$/.test(rest) || /^_/.test(rest)) return { routes: [], page: null };
    return { routes: [], page: segmentsToPath(rest) };
  }
  return { routes: [], page: null };
}
// Entry points from package.json: `bin`, `main`, and `scripts` that run a source file. Node-only (reads files).
import * as fs from 'node:fs';
import { normalizePath, resolvePath } from '../imports';
import type { PackageEntry } from './extract';
import { workspaceDirs } from './resolver';

const RUNNERS = new Set(['node', 'tsx', 'ts-node', 'ts-node-esm', 'bun', 'deno', 'esno', 'esrun', 'vite-node', 'nodemon', 'jiti', 'sucrase-node', 'babel-node']);
const CODE = /\.[cm]?[jt]sx?$/;

type Pkg = { name?: string; bin?: string | Record<string, string>; main?: string; scripts?: Record<string, string> };

/** package.json entries (root and workspace packages) keyed by the repo file they run. */
export function packageEntries(root: string, exists: (path: string) => boolean): Map<string, PackageEntry[]> {
  const out = new Map<string, PackageEntry[]>();
  for (const dir of ['', ...workspaceDirs(root)]) {
    let pkg: Pkg;
    try {
      pkg = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(`${root}/${dir ? `${dir}/` : ''}package.json`, 'utf8')) as Pkg;
    } catch {
      continue;
    }
    const target = (file: string): string | null => {
      const p = normalizePath(dir ? `${dir}/${file}` : file);
      if (!p) return null;
      // Built outputs (`dist/cli.js`) usually come from `src/cli.ts`.
      return resolvePath(p, exists) ?? resolvePath(p.replace(/(^|\/)(?:dist|build|lib|out)\//, '$1src/'), exists);
    };
    const add = (file: string | undefined, entry: PackageEntry) => {
      const t = file ? target(file) : null;
      if (!t) return;
      const list = out.get(t) ?? [];
      if (!list.some((e) => e.kind === entry.kind && e.label === entry.label)) list.push(entry);
      out.set(t, list);
    };
    const name = pkg.name ?? (dir || 'root');
    if (typeof pkg.bin === 'string') add(pkg.bin, { kind: 'bin', label: name.replace(/^@[^/]+\//, '') });
    else for (const [bin, file] of Object.entries(pkg.bin ?? {})) add(file, { kind: 'bin', label: bin });
    if (pkg.main) add(pkg.main, { kind: 'main', label: name });
    for (const [script, cmd] of Object.entries(pkg.scripts ?? {})) {
      const label = dir ? `${name}:${script}` : script;
      for (const part of cmd.split(/&&|\|\||[;|&]/)) {
        const tokens = part.trim().split(/\s+/).filter((t) => !/^\w+=/.test(t)); // drop `FOO=1` env prefixes
        const runner = tokens[0]?.replace(/^npx$/, '') || tokens[1];
        if (!runner || !RUNNERS.has(runner)) continue;
        const file = tokens.find((t) => !t.startsWith('-') && CODE.test(t));
        if (file) add(file, { kind: 'script', label });
      }
    }
  }
  return out;
}
```

You're right that "draw me a diagram" is free, so codemap shouldn't compete on diagram types. What it adds is that the diagram is **checked against the code, clickable through to the code, open to questions, and able to show what's missing**. Any new view should keep those four. A user-journey view keeps them better than I expected.

## Two kinds of "UX help"

Your notes mix two needs, and only one of them fits codemap:

- **UX design** is Jay's problem: mockups side by side, taste, "there's no UX judgement in AI". `HANDOFF.md` already says to leave that out, and I'd still leave it out. It's a different product (21st.dev, v0 and similar).
- **UX comprehension** is Pat's problem: "what happens when the user presses this?", "which pages touch which functions?" His "design bible" is a hand-made journey map that slowly goes out of date. This fits codemap exactly, because every part of a journey can be found in the code.

It also fits your founding story: *"the frontend looked finished… I just trusted what I saw on the frontend."* A journey map puts **what the screen promises** next to **what the code actually does**.

## What a journey map would look like

Here's the care-app fixture as a journey map:

```
 Staff · Patient page                                  Patient · Inbox
┌──────────────────────┐   taps "Mark as converted"   ┌──────────────────┐
│ Patient header       │ ───────────────────────────▶ │ Badge: Converted │
│ [Mark as converted]  │                              └──────────────────┘
└──────────────────────┘                                       ┊
         │ behind this tap ▾                                   ┊ ✗ expects welcome email
         ▼                                                     ┊   nothing sends it
   (opens the system map: POST /convert → markConverted → event → ✗ no listener)
```

- **Areas are screens**, grouped by who's using them (staff or patient). Personas show up here, but only as roles the code knows about (route guards, role checks), not invented ones.
- **Boxes are things a person sees or does**: a button, a form, a message.
- **Arrows are user moves**: "taps Convert", "submits the form", "goes to /billing".
- **"Behind this tap"** on any action opens the existing system map for it. The journey sits on top and the system sits underneath. A non-technical founder reads the top layer, and the technical cofounder drills down. That's the shared language from `HANDOFF.md`.

## How it stays checked

Most journey claims can be proven, and part of the proof already exists:

| Claim | Proof | Status today |
|---|---|---|
| The screen exists | `entry:page` facts (Next.js pages), components | Exists |
| A button calls a handler | `onClick={onConvert}` in the cited line | Text proof works now; a JSX event fact would give fact proof |
| The action hits the backend | fetch → route matching (`request` edges) | **Exists**: `PatientHeader.tsx` → `POST /api/patients/:id/convert` already checks |
| Tapping goes to another screen | `router.push`, `<Link href>`, `navigate()` matched against page entries | New extractor, same pattern as fetch → route |
| What the user sees afterwards | Cited render, toast or state lines | Text proof |

**Gaps you can prove are where the value is.** These are the UX bugs semi-technical builders can't see:

- a button with no handler, or one whose request goes to a route that doesn't exist
- a screen that no navigation leads to, or one that's a dead end
- a form that sends a request but shows nothing when it fails
- something the screen promises ("we'll email you") that nothing in the code does

Each of these is an `Absence` with a search behind it, exactly like the missing listener today.

## What it would change in the format

This is deliberately small, since the format is the one-way door:

- `NodeKind`: add `screen` and `action` (or one `ui` kind with a subtype)
- `EdgeKind`: add `navigates`, proven from router facts
- The map gets `lens: 'system' | 'journey'` (default `system`) so the viewer lays it out as a left-to-right journey instead of nested areas
- Drill-down reuses what exists: an action can link to a system map through `meta.parent`, the same link the "elsewhere" offer uses now

`check()` stays the single checker. It learns one new edge kind and nothing else forks.

## On the bigger vision

"Give the agent tooling to spin up interactive diagrams through codemap" fits the `publish_map` MCP tool already listed in `HANDOFF.md`. The agent explores however it likes, hands codemap a map in one of a few views, and codemap checks it, draws it and makes it askable. My one caution is to **add a view only when most of its claims can be checked**. An unchecked view is just Mermaid with extra steps, and it weakens trust in the checked ones.

- **Journeys pass that test.**
- **Dependency graphs** (Patrick's "remove the GitHub connection") pass it too.
- **Personas as design intent, and "is this architecture scalable"**, don't.

## Suggested next step

1. Give the care-app fixture a two-screen frontend with real navigation, plus one planted UX gap (a button whose route doesn't exist).
2. Add the navigation extractor to `@codemap/facts`.
3. Sketch the journey layout in the viewer.
4. Then show it to Pat and ask: "is this the design bible you made by hand, and would you trust it more if it checked itself?"

Want me to write this up as a design note next to the v1 spec, or start on the fixture and extractor?

```text
# Pages

An artifact is a web page this server hosts at a claude.ai link. These are the rules the server applies.

## What a page is

- One complete HTML document. Begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>: content that does not read as HTML is refused. To publish a Markdown document, write an HTML page from its content.
- A page published as one document carries its own CSS, JavaScript, data and images (data: URIs or inline SVG); only the libraries and fonts listed below load from outside. A page published from files may also load its own files by relative path.
- Give it a <title>. On a new artifact pass the same words as title.
- Put viewport-fit=cover in its viewport meta only with env(safe-area-inset-*) padding: the Claude iOS app draws such a page under its top bar.
- A page can be up to 16 MiB.

## What a page may load

The page runs under a content security policy. Apart from the artifact's own files, anything not listed here is blocked by the browser, with no error on the page.

- Scripts: inline, or from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide/, cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/python-visualization/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com, code.jquery.com, cdn.plot.ly.
- Stylesheets: inline, or from fonts.googleapis.com. A library's stylesheet from any other host must be inlined or shipped as one of the page's own files.
- Fonts: from fonts.gstatic.com (through a Google Fonts stylesheet), or inlined as data: URIs.
- Images and media: data: and blob: URIs. A remote image does not load.
- fetch, XMLHttpRequest and WebSocket to other hosts are blocked.

## What the viewer's frame allows

The page runs in a sandboxed frame.

- Refused or ignored: alert, confirm and prompt; window.print; downloads the page starts, by <a download> or by script; clipboard reads (the viewer's own paste works); camera, microphone, location, motion, screen capture and Web Share; service workers; WebRTC; <object>, <embed> and iframes of other sites. Build dialogs into the page, offer a Copy button where you would offer an export, and offer no button for the others unless a capability (last item) provides it.
- Link to other sites with a plain <a href>, which the viewer opens outside the page; window.open fails for most viewers.
- mailto:, tel: and other non-web links fail for many viewers: keep the link, show the address or number as text too, and never report a message as sent.
- A form has nowhere to submit: handle submit in script, with preventDefault().
- Call these only from a click handler, and catch a refusal: navigator.clipboard.writeText, fullscreen, pointer lock, audio playback.
- These work: file inputs and dropped files (use them in place of the camera and microphone), Web Workers from the page's own files or blob: URLs.
- localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB keep data in one viewer's browser. It survives a republish, reaches no other viewer or device and not Claude, and may be missing or throw: use try/catch and render well without it. Use it only for one viewer's conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, an unsent draft), never for state that must last.
- Only a plain #name passes between the artifact's URL and location.hash, never #/path, #key=value, a pushState path or a query string. The address bar on the artifact's own page and Share's Copy link follow the page's hash; beside a chat, in a project or in an app the bar may not. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending, route on the hash: name each in ASCII letters, digits and hyphens such as #costs-emea (never settings, sidebar, customize, upgrade, downloads or comment-*, which claude.ai reserves) and show the one in location.hash, or the start view if none, on load and on hashchange. Keep other state in the page, and keys, tokens or private values out of the hash: it shows in history and copied links.
- Where this server lists a tool that describes page capabilities, call it before writing a page that needs downloads, a device, state that must last, or data that other viewers or devices must see: a capability may provide it. If none does, tell the user what cannot work, and do not fake it.

## Who can see it

A new artifact is visible to its owner only. This server cannot change who can see an artifact; the owner shares it from its page on claude.ai.

## Publishing

- Where this server lists a tool that publishes from files on disk and you can write files, that is the way to publish a page you write: write the page to a file in your working folder, then publish the file without stopping to ask, with title and icon. You write the page once, and the file is yours to look at and edit later.
- Where it lists none, where you cannot write files, or where that tool answers that the client cannot attach files: publish_version with title, icon and content, no slug.
- Either way the result carries slug, version and url.
- Small change to a page: edit_version with slug, base_version and edits. The server reads the page, replaces each old_text with its new_text, and publishes the result. Nothing is published if an edit does not apply.
- Small change to another text file of an artifact published from files, such as a stylesheet or a script: the same call with path. Every other file is kept. A JSON file must still parse after the edits, or nothing is published.
- Whole new page for an existing artifact: publish it as you would a new page, adding slug and base_version. Whichever way you publish it, the artifact's other files, if it has any, are kept and still served. A publish from files can also remove the ones the new page no longer uses.
- When the artifact's read value is users, org or public, every republish also passes shared_live with that word. It states who the artifact is already shared with and changes nothing.
- base_version is the version you last saw: from your last publish result, get_artifact or read_artifact. If someone published since, the call is refused with a conflict that names the live version. Do what the refusal's error sentence says. If it has none, read the artifact again, redo the change on the current page, and retry; never retry with the new version and your old content.
- Omit title and icon when republishing to keep them. Pass title only to rename.
- read_artifact reads a page the user owns, or one that belongs to someone in the user's organization and that the user can open. Where it refuses a page because of who has written to it, it names read_shared_artifact, and the user is asked first. A page the user does not own can be republished only with edit_version or publish_version, and only if it is in the user's organization, is not public, and the user can edit it.
- To read a page too large for one result, call read_artifact with offset and follow next_offset. A part is never the whole page: do not send it to publish_version.
- After a publish, say in one sentence what the page is, or what changed on a republish, and give the user the url. If your instructions or the publish result say the user's app already shows a card with the page's link, leave the url out unless the user asks for it.
- The published page is the delivery. If you wrote a file, keep it, but do not also send it to the user unless they ask for it.

## What is refused

- Artifacts of another organization, and ones the user does not own and cannot edit.
- Public artifacts the user does not own.
- By publish_version, and by edit_version without path: artifacts made from a type (a slide deck, a document, a design). Where this server offers a tool that publishes from files, it publishes the content files of one whose type keeps content in files, in patch mode, and edit_version with path replaces text in one of them; the type's own files cannot be changed.
- Artifacts that hold a live document.
- Content that is not HTML, or that embeds an archive or a PDF.
```

```text
# Design

Work the way the design lead at a small studio would: make deliberate choices about palette, typography and layout that are specific to this subject.

## Read the request first

Every page is designed; decide only the treatment. A memo gets the same craft as a landing page.

- Many requests call for a utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing and a proper palette, but do not over-design: most pages need no flashy, gigantic hero, and few flourishes.
- Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool the user will keep or share. For those, read the editorial topic too.
- If unsure, a well-composed plain page is always acceptable; an over-designed one sometimes is not.

## Before writing

- If the page, the user or their project has a design system, apply it. The user's own words come first, then that system, then your choices.
- Define the subject, its audience and the page's single job. Use real content, never lorem ipsum. Include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament.
- Settle a short plan and write it into the page as the :root block at the top of its <style>: 4 to 6 named color tokens, font tokens for display and body, the layout idea as a one-line comment. Build the rest from those tokens. Unless the user asks about the design, tell them at most one plain sentence on its direction, with no hex values or font names.

## Name

The <title> is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab. Give it a real name that picks this page out among dozens: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, or the question itself for a page that answers one. No explanation after a dash or a colon. When trimming, keep the identifying word, not the generic one. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use it.

## Type

- Pair a display face, used with restraint, with a body face. Link Google Fonts directly; declare a real fallback stack.
- Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it.
- Give headings text-wrap: balance. Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums where digits line up in columns.

## Color and themes

The page renders in the viewer's theme. The viewer sets data-theme="dark" or data-theme="light" on the root element, or nothing at all, in which case only prefers-color-scheme tells light from dark.

- Define the complete light palette as tokens in the bare :root block, before any media or [data-theme] block redefines them; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug.
- Redefine the tokens under @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark), guarded as :root:not([data-theme="light"]).
- Redefine them again under :root[data-theme="dark"]. Set color-scheme: dark wherever the dark palette applies.
- Style every element through the tokens, never directly inside those blocks.
- Set an explicit background on body from a token. A transparent body shows the host's background.
- Give the second theme the same care: do not simply invert it; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both backgrounds.
- Choose neutrals deliberately: a grey with a slight bias toward the accent reads as intended.
- A page that commits to one visual world may stay single-theme, by choice: omit the media and [data-theme] blocks, and set the background, every color and color-scheme explicitly.

## Layout

- Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and gap, not per-element margins.
- Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width, about 400px.
- Give images max-width: 100%. Only wide tables, code and diagrams may exceed the screen; give each overflow-x: auto on its own container, so the page body never scrolls sideways.
- Size a one-screen app with height: 100% on html and body, not 100vh.
- Make repeated elements consistent: the same edges, baselines and padding on each card or row. Text that outgrows its box wraps or scrolls: clipped text is a bug.
- Use borders, fills, radius and shadow by role, to set off the one element that needs it.

## Complete at rest

Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded: nothing waits for a scroll or a click to appear. That first frame is what a thumbnail and a shared link show. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state, with the user's real data or clearly marked examples, never an empty shell. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at opacity: 0 waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content, not the viewport: a 100vh opener pushes the rest out of that frame.

## Tools and dashboards

These are scanned and operated, not read top to bottom: the craft shifts from typography to information design.

- Put the summary before the detail.
- Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance.
- Semantic color (good, warning, critical) is separate from the accent and does not count as it.
- Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint.
- Interactive elements should look interactive.
- Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

## Libraries and graphics

- Most pages need no library. When one does substantial work, load its UMD build with one <script src> from cdnjs, placed before the inline script that uses it; do not paste its source into the page or write your own version of it. Inline only its stylesheet.
- Pin every library URL to an exact version (react@18.3.1 on jsDelivr or unpkg, react/18.3.1/… on cdnjs, cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17), never a bare name, a range or a tag (react@18, @latest). Choose one at least two weeks old: any you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any from the last two weeks.
- Draw charts to one scale, with every label naming a value the chart reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens. Keep marks and labels clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds.
- For generative or decorative graphics use Canvas, not long hand-written SVG paths.

## Avoid the generic looks

Without a direction from the user, do not fall back on: warm cream with a serif display and a terracotta accent; near-black with one acid-green accent; a purple-to-blue gradient hero; Inter or Space Grotesk as the safe face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; the same rounded card everywhere. When the user asks for one of these, follow them.

## Words

Write from the user's side of the screen. Name things by what people recognize. Use active voice; a control says exactly what happens. Errors say what went wrong and how to fix it. Prefer specific to clever, and short, direct sentences. Avoid mannered devices: em-dash asides, "not X, but Y", colon-then-reveal, scare quotes on invented labels, stock phrases like "worth noting". Numbered markers, eyebrows and dividers must encode something true about the content.

## Build cleanly

Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect prefers-reduced-motion, and give every form control a stable id. Watch selector specificity so one rule does not silently undo another's spacing.

## Write, check once, publish

Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way, such as one screenshot of the file you wrote; otherwise skip the look. Make one pass of edits for what it shows, then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring) may also get one run of a pure function. Never loop, since the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Further polish is for the user to request: if they report something visibly broken, fix that, look at most once more, and republish once.
```

```html
  <div class="checks" aria-label="Check results">
    <span class="pill ok"><span class="dot"></span>17 of 17 steps checked against the code</span>
    <span class="pill gap"><span class="dot"></span>2 things missing</span>
    <span class="pill warn"><span class="dot"></span>1 surprise</span>
  </div>
</header>

<div class="toolbar">
  <div class="seg" role="group" aria-label="View">
    <button id="v-journey" aria-pressed="true">Journey</button>
    <button id="v-screens" aria-pressed="false">Screens</button>
  </div>
  <span class="label">People</span>
  <button class="chip" id="p-staff" aria-pressed="true">Front-desk staff</button>
  <button class="chip" id="p-patient" aria-pressed="true">Patient</button>
  <button class="chip" id="p-system" aria-pressed="true">Behind the scenes</button>
  <span class="spacer"></span>
  <div class="legend">
    <span><i></i>a person's move</span>
    <span><i class="dot"></i>what the tap sets off</span>
    <span><i class="dash"></i>missing</span>
  </div>
</div>

<main>
  <section class="canvas-wrap" id="canvas">
    <div id="journey">
      <div class="stage" id="stage">
        <div class="lane staff" data-lane="staff"><div class="lane-label"><b>Front-desk staff</b><small>Signed in with the staff role</small></div></div>
        <div class="lane patient" data-lane="patient"><div class="lane-label"><b>Patient</b><small>Not signed in yet; reached by email</small></div></div>
        <div class="lane system" data-lane="system"><div class="lane-label"><b>Behind the scenes</b><small>What a tap sets off. Click for code.</small></div></div>
        <svg class="wires" id="wires" aria-hidden="true"></svg>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div id="screens" class="screens hidden">
      <h2>Every screen in this journey, and what it touches</h2>
      <p>The "design bible" view: one row per screen, with the backend it reaches and what's missing. It's rebuilt from the code, so it can't go stale.</p>
      <div class="tablewrap"><table id="screen-table"></table></div>
    </div>
    <div class="tour" id="tour"><span class="label">Walkthrough</span></div>
  </section>

  <aside id="panel" aria-live="polite"></aside>
</main>

<script>
// ---------- Data: what codemap would produce for this journey ----------
const SCREENS = [
  { id: 's-leads', lane: 'staff', x: 150, y: 34, route: '/leads', title: 'Leads list', note: 'Every new enquiry, newest first.',
    thumb: '<div class="bar w40"></div><div class="row"><div class="bar w80"></div></div><div class="row"><span class="hot">Dana Okafor</span><div class="bar w40"></div></div><div class="bar w60"></div>' },
  { id: 's-lead', lane: 'staff', x: 420, y: 34, route: '/patients/:id', title: 'Lead profile', note: 'Contact details and the convert button.',
    thumb: '<div class="row"><div class="bar w40"></div><span class="hot">Mark as converted</span></div><div class="bar w80"></div><div class="bar w60"></div><div class="bar w40"></div>' },
  { id: 's-after', lane: 'staff', x: 720, y: 34, route: '/patients/:id', title: 'Patient profile', note: 'Badge reads "Enrolled".', flag: ['warn', 'Only after a reload'],
    thumb: '<div class="row"><div class="bar w40"></div><span class="badge">Enrolled</span></div><div class="bar w80"></div><div class="bar w60"></div><div class="bar w40"></div>' },
  { id: 's-journeys', lane: 'staff', x: 1010, y: 34, route: '/patients/:id/journeys', title: 'Care journey tab', note: 'Shows "Welcome email: Active".',
    thumb: '<div class="bar w60"></div><div class="row"><div class="bar w40"></div><span class="hot">Welcome email · Active</span></div><div class="bar w80"></div><div class="bar w40"></div>' },
  { id: 's-fail', lane: 'staff', x: 720, y: 222, route: 'error path', title: 'Convert fails', note: 'Server down or the request is rejected.', gap: true, flag: ['gap', 'Nothing tells staff'] , small: true },
  { id: 'p-inbox', lane: 'patient', x: 1010, y: 360, route: 'email', title: 'Welcome email', note: '"Welcome to Northside Clinic"', gap: true, flag: ['gap', 'Never arrives'],
    thumb: '<div class="mail missing">✉ Welcome to Northside Clinic</div><div class="bar w80"></div><div class="bar w60"></div>' },
  { id: 'p-portal', lane: 'patient', x: 1260, y: 360, route: '/portal/sign-in', title: 'Patient portal', note: 'Set a password, see appointments.', unreach: true, flag: ['gap', 'Can’t be reached'],
    thumb: '<div class="bar w40"></div><div class="bar w80"></div><div class="row"><span class="hot gap">Sign in</span></div>' },
];
const SYS = [
  { id: 'c-route', x: 420, y: 588, code: 'POST /convert', sub: 'the app’s server' },
  { id: 'c-mark', x: 600, y: 588, code: 'markConverted()', sub: 'saves status "enrolled"' },
  { id: 'c-event', x: 780, y: 588, code: 'patient.converted', sub: 'announces it happened' },
  { id: 'c-none', x: 960, y: 588, code: 'no listener', sub: 'nobody hears it', gap: true },
  { id: 'c-rules', x: 1140, y: 588, code: 'evaluateRules()', sub: 'would queue the email', idle: true },
];
// [from, fromSide, to, toSide, kind, labelId?]
const WIRES = [
  ['s-leads', 'r', 's-lead', 'l', '', 'm-open'],
  ['s-lead', 'r', 's-after', 'l', '', 'm-convert'],
  ['s-lead', 'b', 's-fail', 'l', 'gap', 'm-fail'],
  ['s-after', 'r', 's-journeys', 'l', '', 'm-tab'],
  ['s-journeys', 'b', 'p-inbox', 't', 'gap', 'm-promise'],
  ['p-inbox', 'r', 'p-portal', 'l', 'muted', 'm-link'],
  ['m-convert', 'b', 'c-route', 't', 'behind'],
  ['c-route', 'r', 'c-mark', 'l', ''],
  ['c-mark', 'r', 'c-event', 'l', ''],
  ['c-event', 'r', 'c-none', 'l', 'gap'],
  ['c-none', 'r', 'c-rules', 'l', 'muted'],
  ['c-none', 't', 'p-inbox', 'b', 'gap'],
];
const MOVES = {
  'm-open': { verb: 'taps', what: 'a lead' },
  'm-convert': { verb: 'taps', what: 'Mark as converted' },
  'm-fail': { verb: 'if it', what: 'fails', gap: true },
  'm-tab': { verb: 'opens', what: 'Journeys' },
  'm-promise': { verb: 'promises', what: 'a welcome email', gap: true },
  'm-link': { verb: 'taps', what: 'sign-in link', muted: true },
};

// What the side panel says for each thing you can select.
const DETAIL = {
  'm-convert': {
    kind: 'A person’s move', title: 'Staff tap “Mark as converted”',
    lede: 'The lead becomes a patient. Staff expect the welcome email to go out on its own, because the Journeys tab says it’s active.',
    chain: [
      ['ok', 'The button sends a request to the server', 'src/ui/PatientHeader.tsx:3'],
      ['ok', 'The server saves the patient as “enrolled”', 'src/patients/service.ts:5'],
      ['ok', 'It announces “patient converted”', 'src/patients/service.ts:6'],
      ['gap', 'Nothing is listening for that announcement', 'search: bus.on(\'patient.converted\' → 0 matches'],
      ['idle', 'So the welcome-email rule never runs', 'src/automations/evaluate.ts:4'],
    ],
    callouts: [
      ['warn', 'The screen doesn’t change after the tap', 'The button sends the request and ignores the reply, so staff see “Enrolled” only after reloading. Many will tap twice.', 'src/ui/PatientHeader.tsx:3 · result unused'],
    ],
    code: { file: 'src/ui/PatientHeader.tsx', lines: [
      [2, 'export function PatientHeader({ patientId }) {'],
      [3, "  const onConvert = () => fetch(`/api/patients/${patientId}/convert`, { method: 'POST' });", true],
      [4, '  return <button onClick={onConvert}>Mark as converted</button>;'],
    ]},
    touches: ['PatientHeader', 'POST /api/patients/:id/convert', 'markConverted', 'patients table', 'patient.converted'],
    ask: ['Why doesn’t the screen update?', 'What should be listening?', 'Who else can convert a patient?'],
  },
  'p-inbox': {
    kind: 'Missing', title: 'The patient never gets a welcome email', gapState: true,
    lede: 'The Journeys tab tells staff the welcome email is active, and the rule that sends it exists. But nothing ever runs that rule after a conversion.',
    callouts: [
      ['gap', 'Nothing listens for “patient converted”', 'The app announces the conversion, but no part of the code is listening for that announcement, so the email rule never runs.', 'searched src/ for bus.on(\'patient.converted\' · 0 matches · re-checked just now'],
    ],
    chain: [
      ['ok', 'Rule “welcome_email” is stored and marked active', 'src/automations/evaluate.ts:5'],
      ['gap', 'No listener connects the conversion to the rule', 'missing'],
      ['idle', 'The email queue would send it overnight', 'src/jobs/queue.ts'],
    ],
    fix: { text: 'Add one line where the app starts up: when a patient is converted, run the automation rules.', diff: "+ bus.on('patient.converted', evaluateRules);" },
    touches: ['patient.converted', 'evaluateRules', 'automation_rules table', 'queueEmail'],
    ask: ['Did this ever work?', 'Would the email send right away or overnight?', 'What else does the portal link depend on?'],
  },
  's-fail': {
    kind: 'Missing', title: 'If converting fails, staff aren’t told', gapState: true,
    lede: 'If the server is down or refuses the request, the button looks exactly as if it worked. Staff move on, and the patient stays a lead.',
    callouts: [
      ['gap', 'No error is ever shown', 'The request’s result is never checked, so there’s no error message, retry or spinner.', 'searched src/ui/PatientHeader.tsx for catch|res.ok|error · 0 matches'],
    ],
    fix: { text: 'Check the reply, show “Couldn’t convert, try again” on failure, and show the new badge on success.', diff: "- const onConvert = () => fetch(url, { method: 'POST' });\n+ const onConvert = async () => {\n+   const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST' });\n+   res.ok ? setStatus('enrolled') : setError('Couldn’t convert. Try again.');\n+ };" },
    touches: ['PatientHeader'],
    ask: ['What errors can the server return here?', 'Is this pattern used on other buttons?'],
  },
  's-after': {
    kind: 'Screen', title: 'Patient profile, after converting',
    lede: 'Same page as before, now with an “Enrolled” badge. The badge comes from the saved status, so it only appears when the page loads again.',
    callouts: [['warn', 'Only after a reload', 'The convert button doesn’t refresh the page or update the badge itself.', 'src/ui/PatientHeader.tsx:3']],
    touches: ['PatientHeader', 'GET /api/patients/:id', 'patients table'],
    ask: ['Where does the badge read its status from?'],
  },
  's-journeys': {
    kind: 'Screen', title: 'Care journey tab',
    lede: 'Lists the automations for this patient. “Welcome email: Active” means the rule is switched on; it doesn’t mean anything will run it.',
    callouts: [['gap', 'This screen promises something the code never does', 'See “The patient never gets a welcome email”.', 'linked gap']],
    touches: ['automation_rules table'],
    ask: ['What does “Active” actually check?'],
  },
  'p-portal': {
    kind: 'Screen', title: 'Patient portal sign-in',
    lede: 'The page exists and works, but the only way in is the link in the welcome email. Since that email never sends, new patients can’t reach it.',
    callouts: [['gap', 'No other way in', 'No other screen links to the portal sign-in.', 'searched src/ for "/portal/sign-in" · 1 match, inside the email template']],
    touches: ['/portal/sign-in'],
    ask: ['Could staff send the link by hand?'],
  },
};
const DEFAULTS = {
  's-leads': ['Screen', 'Leads list', 'Every new enquiry, newest first. Tapping a name opens that lead’s profile.', ['GET /api/leads', 'leads table']],
  's-lead': ['Screen', 'Lead profile', 'Contact details, notes, and the “Mark as converted” button staff press once the person books.', ['PatientHeader', 'GET /api/patients/:id']],
  'm-open': ['A person’s move', 'Staff open a lead', 'A plain link to the lead’s profile page.', ['<Link href="/patients/:id">']],
  'm-tab': ['A person’s move', 'Staff open the Journeys tab', 'Switches tab on the same profile page.', ['JourneysTab']],
  'm-fail': ['What if', 'The convert request fails', 'See “If converting fails, staff aren’t told”.', []],
  'm-promise': ['Promise', 'The tab promises a welcome email', 'Staff read “Active” as “the patient will get the email”. The code doesn’t do that.', []],
  'm-link': ['A person’s move', 'Patient taps the sign-in link', 'Would open the portal, but the email carrying the link never arrives.', []],
  'c-route': ['Behind the scenes', 'POST /api/patients/:id/convert', 'The server address the button calls. It hands off to markConverted.', ['src/server/routes.ts:6']],
  'c-mark': ['Behind the scenes', 'markConverted()', 'Saves the patient’s status as “enrolled”, then announces “patient converted”.', ['src/patients/service.ts:4']],
  'c-event': ['Behind the scenes', 'The “patient converted” announcement', 'A message other parts of the app can listen for. Right now none do.', ['src/patients/service.ts:6', 'src/events/bus.ts:8']],
  'c-none': null, 'c-rules': ['Behind the scenes', 'evaluateRules()', 'Finds active automation rules and queues the welcome email. It exists, but nothing calls it.', ['src/automations/evaluate.ts:4']],
};
DEFAULTS['c-none'] = null;
for (const [id, d] of Object.entries(DEFAULTS)) if (d && !DETAIL[id]) DETAIL[id] = { kind: d[0], title: d[1], lede: d[2], touches: d[3], ask: ['What happens next?'] };
DETAIL['c-none'] = DETAIL['p-inbox'];
DETAIL['m-fail'] = DETAIL['s-fail'];
DETAIL['m-promise'] = DETAIL['p-inbox'];

const TOUR = [
  ['s-leads', 'Where staff start'],
  ['m-convert', 'The convert tap'],
  ['s-fail', 'When it fails'],
  ['s-journeys', 'What the screen promises'],
  ['p-inbox', 'What the patient never gets'],
];

// ---------- Render ----------
const stage = document.getElementById('stage');
const el = (tag, cls, html) => { const e = document.createElement(tag); if (cls) e.className = cls; if (html != null) e.innerHTML = html; return e; };

for (const s of SCREENS) {
  const c = el('button', 'card' + (s.gap ? ' gap' : '') + (s.unreach ? ' unreach' : ''));
  c.id = s.id; c.dataset.lane = s.lane; c.style.left = s.x + 'px'; c.style.top = s.y + 'px';
  c.innerHTML = (s.thumb ? `<div class="thumb">${s.thumb}</div>` : '') +
    `<div class="route">${s.route}</div><h3>${s.title}</h3><div class="note">${s.note}</div>` +
    (s.flag ? `<span class="flag ${s.flag[0]}">${s.flag[0] === 'gap' ? '✕' : '!'} ${s.flag[1]}</span>` : '');
  stage.appendChild(c);
}
for (const s of SYS) {
  const c = el('button', 'sys' + (s.gap ? ' gap' : '') + (s.idle ? ' idle' : ''), `<code>${s.gap ? '✕ ' : ''}${s.code}</code><span>${s.sub}</span>`);
  c.id = s.id; c.dataset.lane = 'system'; c.style.left = s.x + 'px'; c.style.top = s.y + 'px';
  stage.appendChild(c);
}
for (const [id, m] of Object.entries(MOVES)) {
  const b = el('button', 'move' + (m.gap ? ' gap' : '') + (m.muted ? ' muted' : ''), `<span class="verb">${m.verb}</span> ${m.what}`);
  b.id = id; stage.appendChild(b);
}

function anchor(node, side) {
  const x = node.offsetLeft, y = node.offsetTop, w = node.offsetWidth, h = node.offsetHeight;
  const isMove = node.classList.contains('move'); // positioned by its center
  const cx = isMove ? x : x + w / 2, cy = isMove ? y : y + h / 2;
  const hw = w / 2, hh = h / 2;
  return { r: [cx + hw, cy, 1, 0], l: [cx - hw, cy, -1, 0], b: [cx, cy + hh, 0, 1], t: [cx, cy - hh, 0, -1] }[side];
}
function drawWires() {
  const svg = document.getElementById('wires');
  svg.innerHTML = '<defs>' + ['ink', 'gap', 'muted', 'accent'].map((k) =>
    `<marker id="ah-${k}" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" style="fill:var(--${k === 'ink' ? 'ink' : k})"/></marker>`).join('') + '</defs>';
  // Pass 1: wires that carry a label, so labels exist before wires that start from labels.
  const ordered = [...WIRES.filter((w) => w[5]), ...WIRES.filter((w) => !w[5])];
  for (const [from, fs, to, ts, kind, label] of ordered) {
    const a = document.getElementById(from), b = document.getElementById(to);
    if (!a || !b) continue;
    const [x1, y1, nx1, ny1] = anchor(a, fs), [x2, y2, nx2, ny2] = anchor(b, ts);
    const k = Math.max(40, Math.hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1) * 0.35);
    const c1 = [x1 + nx1 * k, y1 + ny1 * k], c2 = [x2 + nx2 * k, y2 + ny2 * k];
    const p = document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'path');
    p.setAttribute('d', `M${x1},${y1} C${c1[0]},${c1[1]} ${c2[0]},${c2[1]} ${x2},${y2}`);
    if (kind) p.setAttribute('class', kind);
    p.dataset.from = from; p.dataset.to = to; if (label) p.dataset.label = label;
    const mk = kind === 'gap' ? 'gap' : kind === 'behind' || kind === 'muted' ? 'muted' : 'ink';
    p.setAttribute('marker-end', `url(#ah-${mk})`);
    svg.appendChild(p);
    if (label) {
      const m = document.getElementById(label);
      const mx = (x1 + 3 * c1[0] + 3 * c2[0] + x2) / 8, my = (y1 + 3 * c1[1] + 3 * c2[1] + y2) / 8;
      m.style.left = mx + 'px'; m.style.top = my + 'px';
    }
  }
  applySelection();
}

// ---------- Selection + panel ----------
let selected = 'm-convert';
const panel = document.getElementById('panel');
function applySelection() {
  document.querySelectorAll('.sel').forEach((n) => n.classList.remove('sel'));
  const node = document.getElementById(selected);
  if (node) node.classList.add('sel');
  document.querySelectorAll('#wires path').forEach((p) => {
    p.classList.toggle('sel', p.dataset.label === selected);
    if (p.classList.contains('sel')) p.setAttribute('marker-end', 'url(#ah-accent)');
  });
  document.querySelectorAll('#tour button').forEach((b) => b.classList.toggle('on', b.dataset.id === selected));
}
function select(id) { selected = id; drawWires(); renderPanel(); }

let tab = 'plain';
function renderPanel() {
  const d = DETAIL[selected];
  if (!d) { panel.innerHTML = ''; return; }
  const chain = d.chain ? `<div><h4>What actually happens</h4><ol class="chain">${d.chain.map(([s, t, c]) =>
    `<li class="${s}"><span class="mk">${s === 'ok' ? '✓' : s === 'gap' ? '✕' : '–'}</span><div><div class="t">${t}</div><div class="c">${c}</div></div></li>`).join('')}</ol></div>` : '';
  const callouts = (d.callouts || []).map(([k, b, t, proof]) => `<div class="callout ${k}"><b>${b}</b>${t}<span class="proof">${proof}</span></div>`).join('');
  const fix = d.fix ? `<div><h4>Suggested fix</h4><p class="lede" style="margin-bottom:8px">${d.fix.text}</p><div class="codeblk">${esc(d.fix.diff)}</div>
    <div class="actions" style="margin-top:8px"><button class="btn primary" id="preview-fix">Preview on the map</button><button class="btn">Hand to my coding agent</button></div></div>` : '';
  const code = d.code ? `<div><span class="cite">${d.code.file}</span><div class="codeblk">${d.code.lines.map(([n, t, hl]) =>
    `<span class="${hl ? 'hl' : ''}"><span class="ln">${String(n).padStart(2)}  </span>${esc(t)}</span>`).join('\n')}</div></div>` : '';
  const touches = d.touches && d.touches.length ? `<div><h4>What this touches</h4><div class="touches">${d.touches.map((t) => `<span>${esc(t)}</span>`).join('')}</div></div>` : '';
  const body = tab === 'plain' ? `${callouts}${chain}${fix}` : `${code || '<p class="mock">Code for this step opens here, with the cited lines highlighted.</p>'}${touches}`;
  panel.innerHTML = `
    <div class="kind">${d.gapState ? '<span class="pill gap"><span class="dot"></span>Missing</span>' : esc(d.kind)}</div>
    <h2>${esc(d.title)}</h2>
    <p class="lede">${esc(d.lede)}</p>
    <div class="tabs" role="tablist"><button role="tab" id="t-plain" aria-selected="${tab === 'plain'}">Plain English</button><button role="tab" id="t-code" aria-selected="${tab === 'code'}">Code</button></div>
    ${body}
    <div class="ask"><h4 style="margin:0">Ask about this step</h4>
      <div class="sugg">${(d.ask || []).map((q) => `<button>${esc(q)}</button>`).join('')}</div>
      <form id="ask-form"><input id="ask-input" placeholder="Ask anything about “${esc(d.title)}”" aria-label="Your question"><button class="btn">Ask</button></form>
      <div id="reply"></div>
    </div>`;
  panel.querySelector('#t-plain').onclick = () => { tab = 'plain'; renderPanel(); };
  panel.querySelector('#t-code').onclick = () => { tab = 'code'; renderPanel(); };
  panel.querySelectorAll('.sugg button').forEach((b) => (b.onclick = () => answer(b.textContent)));
  panel.querySelector('#ask-form').onsubmit = (e) => { e.preventDefault(); const v = panel.querySelector('#ask-input').value.trim(); if (v) answer(v); };
  const pf = panel.querySelector('#preview-fix');
  if (pf) pf.onclick = () => { panel.querySelector('#reply').innerHTML = '<div class="reply">On the real map, the missing arrow turns into a green dashed one with this change attached. Nothing is written until you approve it.</div>'; };
}
function answer(q) {
  panel.querySelector('#reply').innerHTML = `<div class="reply"><b>${esc(q)}</b><br>In codemap, the answer appears here, next to this step. Anything it adds to the map is checked against the code first.</div><div class="mock">Mockup: no real answers.</div>`;
}
function esc(s) { return String(s).replace(/[&<>"]/g, (c) => ({ '&': '&amp;', '<': '&lt;', '>': '&gt;', '"': '&quot;' }[c])); }

stage.addEventListener('click', (e) => { const t = e.target.closest('.card, .sys, .move'); if (t) select(t.id); });

// ---------- Tour ----------
const tourEl = document.getElementById('tour');
TOUR.forEach(([id, label], i) => {
  const b = el('button', '', `<span class="n">${i + 1}</span>${label}`); b.dataset.id = id;
  b.onclick = () => { showView('journey'); select(id); document.getElementById(id).scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest', inline: 'center', behavior: 'smooth' }); };
  tourEl.appendChild(b);
});

// ---------- People filters ----------
for (const lane of ['staff', 'patient', 'system']) {
  const chip = document.getElementById('p-' + lane);
  chip.onclick = () => {
    const on = chip.getAttribute('aria-pressed') !== 'true';
    chip.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(on));
    document.querySelectorAll(`[data-lane="${lane}"]`).forEach((n) => n.classList.toggle('dim', !on));
  };
}

// ---------- Screens table ----------
const ROWS = [
  ['Leads list', '/leads', 'Staff', 'Open a lead', 'GET /api/leads', 'leads', ''],
  ['Lead profile', '/patients/:id', 'Staff', 'Mark as converted', 'POST /api/patients/:id/convert → markConverted', 'patients (writes status)', '<span class="flag gap">✕ No error shown on failure</span><br><span class="flag warn">! Screen doesn’t update</span>'],
  ['Care journey tab', '/patients/:id/journeys', 'Staff', 'Toggle an automation', 'GET /api/automations', 'automation_rules', '<span class="flag gap">✕ “Active” rule never runs</span>'],
  ['Welcome email', 'email', 'Patient', 'Tap sign-in link', 'evaluateRules → queueEmail → sendEmail', 'email queue', '<span class="flag gap">✕ Never sent</span>'],
  ['Patient portal', '/portal/sign-in', 'Patient', 'Set password', 'POST /api/portal/session', 'patients', '<span class="flag gap">✕ Only reachable from the email</span>'],
];
document.getElementById('screen-table').innerHTML =
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-04 20:17:44Z)**_

My recommendation: **ship the backend version as it is, clean up only what would break a session on a stranger's repo, and test the journey idea with the mockup in the same sessions.** Don't build the journey view yet.

## Why not build both now

- **The journey view isn't a small add-on.** It needs a navigation extractor, new box and arrow kinds in the format, a new layout and a new fixture, so a week or two at least. If the backend map turns out not to be useful, that work rests on a base you haven't validated.
- **The two share the same core.** What makes either one valuable is a map that's checked against the code and can show what's missing. If people don't care about that on the backend map, a journey map won't fix it. If they do care, the journey view becomes an easy extension instead of a new bet.
- **The mockup can do the journey's testing for free.** You don't need working code to learn whether Pat says "that's my design bible."

## The honest risk to the backend version

Your own notes point at it. Patrick doesn't care how things are wired. Pat said "you don't often need to understand what goes on in the backend, but when you do it's tough." So the backend need is probably **occasional but painful**, not daily.

That's fine for a product, but it changes how you test:

- **Test at the moment of need,** with a real question the person has right now, on their own repo. A tour of the care-app fixture won't tell you much.
- **Pick people who hit that moment often.** The integration consultant is the best candidate, since every new client codebase is that moment.

## What to clean up before testing

Only fix what would stop a session:

1. **Run it on a real repo you didn't write** (the Scout copy in `HANDOFF.md`). Big repos are untested, and the head-start scan reads the whole repo. That's the most likely thing to break in front of someone.
2. **Make first-run setup something a stranger can get through.**
3. **Fix any confusing moments** that show up in that dry run. Leave visual polish alone.

## How to run each session (about 30 minutes)

1. Ask them for a real question about their codebase.
2. Ask Claude for a Mermaid diagram of the same question (the free alternative), then run codemap. This is Phase 0 from `HANDOFF.md`.
3. Watch for:
   - whether they click through to the code
   - whether they ask a follow-up on the map
   - whether a "nothing does X" gap surprises them
   - whether they trust it more than the Mermaid diagram, and can say why
4. At the end, show the journey mockup and ask: "Which of these would you open next week?"

## How to decide after about 5 sessions

- **Backend maps win if** people have a real need, prefer codemap to Mermaid for a reason they can name, and want to run it again. Keep going, and build the journey view on top later.
- **The journey wins if** people are lukewarm on the backend map but light up at the mockup. Pivot the front door to journeys and keep the checker. Very little is lost, because the checker, the format, gaps and fixes all carry over.
- **Neither wins if** people say "Mermaid was fine." That's the most important result, and you'd get it in a week instead of a month.

One reframe: the journey and the backend map may not be competing directions at all. Your founding problem was "the frontend looked finished but the backend wasn't wired." The journey could end up being how people find their way into the backend maps.

I can start the dry run on the Scout copy now to see what breaks on a real repo. Or I can write the session script and checklist so you have them ready for the first tester.

I think your read is right, and the audience point is the stronger argument. "People who care about architecture and have big systems" mostly means experienced engineers. They're harder to find, they already hold the model in their heads, and they have other tools. The semi-technical people who build with agents are the ones growing fastest, and they're the ones telling you about UX pain without being asked. I'd lean toward UX.

One check before you commit: **"models are bad at UX" covers two different problems, and codemap only fits one of them.**

| The pain | Example | Fits codemap? |
|---|---|---|
| **It looks bad** (visual taste, layout, polish) | Jay comparing mockups side by side, 21st.dev | No. That's v0 / 21st territory, and a checker adds nothing. |
| **The flow is wrong** (dead ends, missing error or loading states, too many steps, a screen promising something the code doesn't do) | the failed convert that shows nothing; the email that never arrives | **Yes.** These are provable from the code, and the gaps are the bugs. |
| **I can't see what the agent built** without clicking through everything | Pat letting it run for an hour and getting the wrong thing | **Yes.** A journey map of what exists, regenerated after each run. |
| **Iteration is slow** | Jay's loop of re-prompting and re-fixing | Partly. Pointing at a step and saying "change this" is faster than describing it. |

Jay's pain sounds mostly like the first row. Pat's sounds like the second and third rows (user flows, personas, a design bible, seeing what got built). Before building, find out which row each of the three of you is actually in. If it's mostly the first row, that's a different product. If it's the second and third, it's codemap with a better front door.

## What you keep if you pivot

Almost everything: the checker, the format, gaps proven by a rerunnable search, the Ask box, fixes, and Claude explores while the code decides. The backend map becomes the "behind this tap" layer under each user action, so the work isn't thrown away. It's just no longer the first thing people see. That fits your founding story too ("the frontend looked finished, the backend wasn't wired").

Yes, I think there's a real group of people with this problem. Your two examples also show who they are, which is more precise than "people who care about architecture."

**The dividing line is whether breakage costs you something.** Look at your own interviews:

- **Patrick said it himself:** he doesn't care because he has a few users and holds their hands. With 2,000 users, it would matter.
- **Pat** builds things where 80% working is fine.
- **Your workflow builder** was at a job, where it had to actually work and someone else relied on it.
- **The integration consultant** works in a client's codebase, so he's accountable for it.
- **Jay** worries about V2 and V3 because he's betting a company on it.

So the group is **people who build with agents and are on the hook when it breaks**: engineers shipping agent-written features at work, consultants and agencies in client code, and startups past their first handful of users. Pat and Patrick aren't wrong about their own needs. They just aren't on the hook yet, and everyone in the first group got there by gaining users or taking a job.

**Your two examples fit the product differently:**

- **The workflow builder fits well.** "It seemed to work, but I didn't know how it was wired or whether it would hold up" is the same problem as the EHR story and the care-app demo. Codemap v1 is built for it.
- **The overfitted Relu harness only half fits.** A map would show you how the harness works now. It wouldn't tell you "this was patched for one specific error, five times over." That's the band-aid detector on the "later" list in `HANDOFF.md`. It's a real problem, but don't sell it until the product catches it. It's worth finding out whether the current map makes the overfitting visible anyway, for example a tangle of special-case branches all hanging off one step.

**How to check it's not just you:**

1. **Point codemap at your own two cases first.** Relu is the easiest to try. For the workflow builder, check your employer's policy first, since codemap sends code to Claude. Ask the question you actually had back then. If the map doesn't answer it better than you managed at the time, nobody else will be impressed either.
2. **Your coworkers are the easiest test group you have.** They ship agent-written code into a shared codebase and are accountable for it. Ask two or three of them: "When did you last need to understand how something was wired, and what did you do?" If they remember a recent time and what they did was painful, that's your answer.
3. **Then the consultant,** with his real client question, codemap next to Claude + Mermaid.

The question to answer isn't whether these people exist. It's whether they'd use codemap instead of just asking Claude when the moment comes. Your own two cases are the quickest place to find out.
